questions.question: In mirror/substitution coding where the alphabet is reflected around its center, what is always true of a mapped letter pair's positions?
options: They are always identical
They always sum to 27
They always differ by exactly 13
There is no fixed relationship between them
questions.rationale: Mirror coding reflects each letter's position p to position 27-p, so a mapped pair's positions always sum to 27 — the same rule covered in the letter-position and reverse-alphabet sections.

questions.question: Why should you verify a suspected coding rule against every letter of the given example rather than just the first one or two?
options: It isn't necessary once the first letter matches
Some questions apply a non-uniform rule or an exception on a specific letter, which only shows up later in the word
Verification is only needed for number coding, not letter coding
The rule always changes after the third letter
questions.rationale: As the guide's solving-algorithm section stresses, a rule that fits the first letters can still fail on a later one if the question mixes a shift with an exception — full verification catches this before you misapply the rule to the new word.

questions.question: In Polybius/matrix-style coding, what does a letter's code typically represent?
options: Its alphabet position doubled
Its row-and-column coordinate in a grid
The sum of the letters before it
Its mirror letter's position
questions.rationale: Matrix/Polybius-style coding places letters in a grid and encodes each one as a (row, column) coordinate pair rather than a single shifted letter or number.

questions.question: What is the recommended first step in the guide's coding-solving algorithm, before testing any specific rule type?
options: Guess the answer directly from the options
Read all the given examples and separate input from output for each one
Assume a +1 letter shift, since it is the most common rule
Convert every letter straight to a number
questions.rationale: The solving algorithm starts by reading all given examples and separating input from output, so the rule can be compared consistently across every example before it is applied to the new case.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'Final Checklist' at the very end of the lesson?
options: To introduce brand-new rule types
To provide a quick list of essential checks (like verifying the rule against every example, checking wrap-around) to run through before finalizing an answer
To replace the master formula sheet
To only apply to the Expert practice tier
questions.rationale: The Final Checklist provides a quick, essential set of checks — like full verification and wrap-around confirmation — to run through before finalizing any answer.

questions.question: What is likely meant by the lesson's 'Final Concept,' given its recurring themes throughout?
options: That guessing is an acceptable strategy
That reliable coding-decoding solving comes from systematically identifying and verifying a rule against ALL given data, not from guessing after a partial match
That only the simplest rules ever appear
That verification is optional once a pattern seems obvious
questions.rationale: Consistent with the lesson's recurring emphasis, the Final Concept reinforces that reliability comes from systematic identification and full verification, not from guessing after only a partial match.

questions.question: What is the benefit of a 'One-Line Master Rule' summarizing the entire lesson?
options: It replaces the need to understand any individual technique
It distills the single most important principle (like 'find the simplest rule that fits every example') into an instantly recallable form
It has no practical benefit
It only applies to matrix coding
questions.rationale: A one-line master rule distills the single most important overarching principle into a compact, instantly recallable form for quick use.

questions.question: Why does this 22-part lesson end with condensed algorithms and checklists rather than new coding rule types?
options: Because there was no more content to teach
Because every necessary rule type has already been introduced across the earlier parts, and the focus now shifts to consolidation and reliable execution
Because rule types are considered unimportant by this point
Because the lesson ran out of space
questions.rationale: By this point, every necessary rule type has already been thoroughly introduced — the closing sections appropriately shift focus to consolidation and reliable execution.

questions.question: According to the lesson's overall progression, what is the ultimate skill being built across all 22 parts?
options: Memorizing every specific example verbatim
The ability to reliably identify, verify, and apply the correct coding-decoding rule to any new problem, not just memorize specific examples
Only recognizing letter-shift coding
Avoiding verification to save time
questions.rationale: The ultimate goal across all 22 parts is building the ability to reliably identify, verify, and apply the correct rule to ANY new problem — not simply memorizing the specific examples covered.

questions.question: Why is verifying a candidate rule against EVERY given example (not just the first) emphasized so consistently throughout this lesson?
options: Because it is unnecessary in most cases
Because a rule that only explains part of the data can still be wrong overall, and this is one of the most common sources of error in coding-decoding
Because the first example is always sufficient
Because later examples are never actually relevant
questions.rationale: Full verification is emphasized consistently because a rule that only explains part of the data can still be incorrect overall — this remains one of the most common and persistent sources of error.

questions.question: What common thread connects the final exam algorithm to the earlier 'golden rule' (Part 12) about preferring the simplest consistent rule?
options: They are unrelated ideas from different lessons
Both emphasize that reliability comes from systematic verification against all data, not from settling for the first plausible-looking pattern
Both recommend ignoring verification entirely
Both only apply to number-based coding
questions.rationale: Both the golden rule and the final exam algorithm share the same core theme: reliability comes from systematic, full verification, not from settling for the first pattern that seems to fit.

questions.question: Why might the lesson's final checklist explicitly include a wrap-around check, even this late in the lesson?
options: Wrap-around only matters in the earliest parts
Because forgetting wrap-around remains one of the most common and persistent errors, even for learners who understand the more advanced techniques
Because wrap-around checks are no longer relevant by this point
Because wrap-around only applies to matrix coding
questions.rationale: Even after mastering advanced techniques, forgetting basic wrap-around remains a common, persistent error — which is exactly why it's still explicitly included in the final checklist.

questions.question: What is the overarching lesson of this entire 22-part chapter on coding-decoding?
options: That coding-decoding is purely a matter of memorized tricks

That reliably solving coding-decoding problems comes from systematically identifying a rule, verifying it against every given example, and correctly applying (or inverting) it — not from memorizing isolated tricks alone
That only the simplest coding types are ever tested
That verification can safely be skipped once a rule seems obvious
questions.rationale: The chapter's consistent, central lesson is that reliable coding-decoding solving comes from systematic rule identification, full verification, and correct application (or inversion) — not from memorizing isolated tricks alone.
